#Text= 114.
#Text=Non-proteid Animal Foods.
#Text=Butter is one of the most digestible
#Text= of animal fats, agreeable and delicate in flavor, and is on this account
#Text= much used as a wholesome food.
#Text=Various substitutes have recently come into
#Text= use.
#Text=These are all made from animal fat, chiefly that of beef, and are
#Text= known as butterine, oleomargarine, and by other trade names.
#Text=These
#Text= preparations, if properly made, are wholesome, and may be useful
#Text= substitutes for butter, from which they differ but little in composition.
#Text=
#Text= 115.
#Text=Garden Vegetables.
#Text=Various green, fresh, and succulent
#Text= vegetables form an essential part of our diet.
#Text=They are of importance
#Text= not so much on account of their nutritious elements, which are usually
#Text=small, as for the salts they supply, especially the salts of potash.
#Text=It is
#Text= a well-known fact that the continued use of a diet from which fresh
#Text= vegetables are excluded leads to a disease known as scurvy.
#Text=They are also
#Text= used for the agreeable flavor possessed by many, and the pleasant variety
#Text= and relish they give to the food.
#Text=The undigested residue left by all green
#Text= vegetables affords a useful stimulus to intestinal contraction, and tends
#Text= to promote the regular action of the bowels.
#Text=
#Text= 116.
#Text=Fruits.
#Text=A great variety of fruits, both fresh and dry, is
#Text= used as food, or as luxuries.
#Text=They are of little nutritive value,
#Text= containing, as they do, much water and only a small amount of proteid, but
#Text= are of use chiefly for the sugar, vegetable acids, and salts they contain.
#Text=In moderate quantity, fruits are a useful addition to our regular diet.
#Text=They are cooling and refreshing, of agreeable flavor, and tend to prevent
#Text= constipation.
#Text=Their flavor and juiciness serve to stimulate a weak
#Text= appetite and to give variety to an otherwise heavy diet.
#Text=If eaten in
#Text= excess, especially in an unripe or an overripe state, fruits may occasion
#Text= a disturbance of the stomach and bowels, often of a severe form.
#Text=
#Text=117.
#Text=Condiments.
#Text=The refinements of cookery as well as the craving
#Text= of the appetite, demand many articles which cannot be classed strictly as
#Text= foods.
#Text=They are called condiments, and as such may be used in
#Text= moderation.
#Text=They give flavor and relish to food, excite appetite and
#Text= promote digestion.
#Text=Condiments increase the pleasure of eating, and by
#Text= their stimulating properties promote secretions of the digestive fluids
#Text= and excite the muscular contractions of the alimentary canal.
#Text=The well-known condiments are salt, vinegar, pepper, ginger, nutmeg,
#Text= cloves, and various substances containing ethereal oils and aromatics.
#Text=Their excessive use is calculated to excite irritation and disorder of the
#Text= digestive organs.
#Text=
#Text= 118.
#Text=Salt The most important and extensively used of the condiments
#Text= is common salt.
#Text=It exists in all ordinary articles of diet, but in
#Text= quantities not sufficient to meet the wants of the bodily tissues.
#Text=Hence
#Text= it is added to many articles of food.
#Text=It improves their flavor, promotes
#Text= certain digestive secretions, and meets the nutritive demands of the body.
#Text=The use of salt seems based upon an instinctive demand of the system for
#Text= something necessary for the full performance of its functions.

#Text= 120.
#Text=Tea, Coffee, and Cocoa.
#Text=The active principle of tea is called
#Text= theine; that of coffee, caffeine, and of cocoa, theobromine.
#Text=They also
#Text= contain an aromatic, volatile oil, to which they owe their distinctive
#Text= flavor.
#Text=Tea and coffee also contain an astringent called tannin, which
#Text= gives the peculiar bitter taste to the infusions when steeped too long.
#Text=In
#Text= cocoa, the fat known as cocoa butter amounts to fifty per cent.
#Text=
#Text= 121.
#Text=Tea.
#Text=It has been estimated that one-half of the human race now
#Text= use tea, either habitually or occasionally.
#Text=Its use is a prolific source
#Text= of indigestion, palpitation of the heart, persistent wakefulness, and of
#Text= other disorders.
#Text=When used at all it should be only in moderation.
#Text=Persons
#Text= who cannot use it without feeling its hurtful effects, should leave it
#Text= alone.
#Text=It should not be taken on an empty stomach, nor sipped after every
#Text= mouthful of food.
#Text=
#Text= 122.
#Text=Coffee.
#Text=Coffee often disturbs the rhythm of the heart and causes
#Text= palpitation.
#Text=Taken at night, coffee often causes wakefulness.

#Text=Beer and other malt liquors are made from grain.
#Text=By sprouting the grain,
#Text= which changes its starch to sugar, and then dissolving out the sugar with
#Text= water, a sweet liquid is obtained which is fermented with yeast, one kind
#Text= of alcoholic ferment.
#Text=Some kinds of beer contain only a small percentage
#Text= of alcohol, but these are usually drunk in proportionately large amounts.
#Text=The life insurance company finds the beer drinker a precarious risk; the
#Text= surgeon finds him an unpromising subject; the criminal court finds him
#Text= conspicuous in its proceedings.
#Text=The united testimony from all these
#Text= sources is that beer is demoralizing, mentally, morally, and physically.

#Text= 127.
#Text=Cooking.
#Text=The process through which nearly all food used by
#Text= civilized man has to pass before it is eaten is known as cooking.
#Text=Very few articles indeed are consumed in their natural state, the
#Text= exceptions being eggs, milk, oysters, fruit and a few vegetables.
#Text=Man is
#Text= the only animal that cooks his food.
#Text=Although there are savage races that
#Text= have no knowledge of cooking, civilized man invariably cooks most of his
#Text= food.
#Text=It seems to be true that as nations advance in civilization they
#Text= make a proportionate advance in the art of cooking.
#Text=Cooking answers most important purposes in connection with our food,
#Text= especially from its influence upon health.
#Text=It enables food to be more
#Text= readily chewed, and more easily digested.
#Text=Thus, a piece of meat when raw
#Text= is tough and tenacious, but if cooked the fibers lose much of their
#Text= toughness, while the connective tissues are changed into a soft and
#Text= jelly-like mass.
#Text=Besides, the meat is much more readily masticated and
#Text= acted upon by the digestive fluids.
#Text=So cooking makes vegetables and grains
#Text= softer, loosens their structure, and enables the digestive juices readily
#Text= to penetrate their substance.
#Text=Cooking also improves or develops flavors in food, especially in animal
#Text= foods, and thus makes them attractive and pleasant to the palate.
#Text=The
#Text= appearance of uncooked meat, for example, is repulsive to our taste, but
#Text=by the process of cooking, agreeable flavors are developed which stimulate
#Text= the appetite and the flow of digestive fluids.
#Text=Another important use of cooking is that it kills any minute parasites or
#Text= germs in the raw food.
#Text=The safeguard of cooking thus effectually removes
#Text= some important causes of disease.
#Text=The warmth that cooking imparts to food
#Text= is a matter of no slight importance; for warm food is more readily
#Text= digested, and therefore nourishes the body more quickly.
#Text=The art of cooking plays a very important part in the matter of health,
#Text= and thus of comfort and happiness.
#Text=Badly cooked and ill-assorted foods are
#Text= often the cause of serious disorders.
#Text=Mere cooking is not enough, but good
#Text= cooking is essential.

#Text= 165.
#Text=The Kinds of Food Required.
#Text=An appetite for plain, well-cooked
#Text= food is a safe guide to follow.
#Text=Every person in good health, taking a
#Text= moderate amount of daily exercise, should have a keen appetite for three
#Text= meals a day and enjoy them.
#Text=Food should be both nutritious and digestible.
#Text=It is nutritious in proportion to the amount of material it furnishes for
#Text= the nourishment of the tissues.
#Text=It is digestible in a greater or less
#Text= degree in respect to the readiness with which it yields to the action of
#Text= the digestive fluids, and is prepared to be taken up by the blood.
#Text=This
#Text= digestibility depends partly upon the nature of the food in its raw state,
#Text= partly upon the effect produced upon it by cooking, and to some extent
#Text= upon its admixture with other foods.
#Text=Certain foods, as the vegetable

#Text=
#Text= 166.
#Text=Hints about Meals.
#Text=On an average, three meals each day, from
#Text= five to six hours apart, is the proper number for adults.
#Text=Five hours is by
#Text= no means too long a time to intervene between consecutive meals, for it is
#Text= not desirable to introduce new food into the stomach, until the gastric
#Text= digestion of the preceding meal has been completed, and until the stomach
#Text= has had time to rest, and is in condition to receive fresh material.
#Text=The
#Text= stomach, like other organs, does its work best at regular periods.[25]
#Text=
#Text= Eating out of mealtimes should be strictly avoided, for it robs the
#Text= stomach of its needed rest.
#Text=Food eaten when the body and mind are wearied
#Text= is not well digested.
#Text=Rest, even for a few minutes, should be taken before
#Text= eating a full meal.
#Text=It is well to lie down, or sit quietly and read,
#Text= fifteen minutes before eating, and directly afterwards, if possible.
#Text=Severe exercise and hard study just after a full meal, are very apt to
#Text= delay or actually arrest digestion, for after eating heartily, the vital
#Text=forces of the body are called upon to help the stomach digest its food.
#Text=If
#Text= our bodily energies are compelled, in addition to this, to help the
#Text= muscles or brain, digestion is retarded, and a feeling of dullness and
#Text= heaviness follows.
#Text=Fermentative changes, instead of the normal digestive
#Text= changes, are apt to take place in the food.
#Text=
#Text= 167.
#Text=Practical Points about Eating.
#Text=We should not eat for at least
#Text= two or three hours before going to bed.
#Text=When we are asleep, the vital
#Text= forces are at a low ebb, the process of digestion is for the time nearly
#Text= suspended, and the retention of incompletely digested food in the stomach
#Text= may cause bad dreams and troubled sleep.
#Text=But in many cases of
#Text= sleeplessness, a trifle of some simple food, especially if the stomach
#Text= seems to feel exhausted, often appears to promote sleep and rest.

#Text=317.
#Text=The Organ of Taste.
#Text=The sense of taste is located chiefly
#Text= in the tongue, but may also be referred even to the regions of the fauces.
#Text=Taste, like touch, consists in a particular mode of nerve termination.
#Text=The tongue is a muscular organ covered with mucous membrane, and is
#Text= richly supplied with blood-vessels and nerves.
#Text=By its complicated
#Text= movements it is an important factor in chewing, in swallowing, and in
#Text= articulate speech.
#Text=The surface of the tongue is covered with irregular
#Text= projections, called papillæ,--fine hair-like processes, about 1/12 of
#Text= an inch high.
#Text=Interspersed with these are the fungiform papillæ.
#Text=These are shaped something like a mushroom, and may often be detected by
#Text= their bright red points when the rest of the tongue is coated.
#Text=Towards the root of the tongue is another kind of papillæ, the
#Text= circumvallate, eight to fifteen in number, arranged in the form of
#Text= the letter V, with the apex directed backwards.
#Text=These are so called
#Text= because they consist of a fungiform papilla surrounded by a fold of mucous
#Text= membrane, presenting the appearance of being walled around.
#Text=In many of the fungiform and most of the circumvallate papillæ are
#Text=peculiar structures called taste buds or taste goblets.
#Text=These
#Text= exist in great numbers, and are believed to be connected with nerve
#Text= fibers.
#Text=These taste buds are readily excited by savory substances, and
#Text= transmit the impression along the connected nerve.
#Text=The tongue is supplied with sensory fibers by branches from the fifth and
#Text= eighth pairs of cranial nerves.
#Text=The former confers taste on the front part
#Text= of the tongue, and the latter on the back part.
#Text=Branches of the latter
#Text= also pass to the soft palate and neighboring parts and confer taste on
#Text= them.
#Text=The motor nerve of the tongue is the ninth pair, the hypoglossal.

#Text= B, glands at the base of tongue;

#Text=
#Text= 318.
#Text=The Sense of Taste.
#Text=The sense of taste is excited by stimulation
#Text= of the mucous membrane of the tongue and of the palate, affecting the ends
#Text= of the nerve fibers.
#Text=Taste is most acute in or near the circumvallate
#Text= papillæ.
#Text=The middle of the tongue is scarcely sensitive to taste, while
#Text= the edges and the tip are, as a rule, highly sensitive.
#Text=Certain conditions are necessary that the sense of taste may be
#Text= exercised.
#Text=First, the substance to be tasted must be in _solution_, or be
#Text= soluble in the fluids of the mouth.
#Text=Insoluble substances are tasteless.
#Text=If
#Text= we touch our tongue to a piece of rock crystal, there is a sensation of
#Text= contact or cold, but no sense of taste.
#Text=On the other hand, when we bring
#Text= the tongue in contact with a piece of rock salt, we experience the
#Text= sensations of contact, coolness, and saline taste.
#Text=Again, the mucous membrane of the mouth must be _moist_.
#Text=When the mouth is
#Text= dry, and receives substances not already in solution, there is no saliva
#Text= ready to dissolve them; hence, they are tasteless.
#Text=This absence of taste
#Text=is common with the parched mouth during a fever.
#Text=The tongue assists in bringing the food in contact with the nerves, by
#Text= pressing it against the roof of the mouth and the soft palate, and thus is
#Text= produced the fullest sense of taste.
#Text=
#Text= 319.
#Text=Physiological Conditions of Taste.
#Text=The tongue is the seat of
#Text= sensations which are quite unlike each other.
#Text=Thus, besides the sense of
#Text= taste, there is the sensation of touch, pressure, heat and cold, burning
#Text= or acrid feelings, and those produced by the application of the tongue to
#Text= an interrupted electric current.
#Text=These are distinct sensations, due to
#Text= some chemical action excited probably in the touch cells, although the
#Text= true tastes may be excited by causes not strictly chemical.
#Text=Thus a smart
#Text= tap on the tongue may excite the sensation of taste.
#Text=In the majority of persons the back of the tongue is most sensitive to
#Text= bitters, and the tip to sweets.
#Text=Saline matters are perceived most
#Text= distinctly at the tip, and acid substances at the sides.
#Text=The nerves of
#Text= taste are sensitive in an extraordinary degree to some articles of food
#Text= and certain drugs.
#Text=For example, the taste of the various preparations of
#Text=quinine, peppermint, and wild cherry is got rid of with difficulty.
#Text=Like the other special senses, that of taste may become fatigued.
#Text=The
#Text= repeated tasting of one substance rapidly deadens the sensibility,
#Text= probably by over-stimulation.
#Text=Some savors so impress the nerves of taste
#Text= that others fail to make any impression.
#Text=This principle is used to make
#Text= disagreeable medicine somewhat tasteless.
#Text=Thus a few cloves, or grains of
#Text= coffee, or a bit of pepper, eaten before a dose of castor oil, renders it
#Text= less nauseous.
#Text=Flavor is something more than taste.
#Text=It is in reality a mixed
#Text= sensation, in which smell and taste are both concerned, as is shown by the
#Text= common observation that one suffering from a cold in the head, which
#Text= blunts his sense of smell, loses the proper flavor of his food.
#Text=So if a
#Text= person be blindfolded, and the nose pinched, he will be unable to
#Text= distinguish between an apple and an onion, if one be rubbed on the tongue
#Text= after the other.
#Text=As soon as the nostrils are opened the difference is at
#Text= once perceived.
#Text=Experiment 142.
#Text=Put a drop of vinegar on a friend  '  s tongue, or on
#Text=your own.
#Text=Notice how the papillæ of the tongue start up.
#Text=Experiment 143.
#Text=Rub different parts of the tongue with the pointed
#Text= end of a piece of salt or gum-aloes, to show that the _back_ of the
#Text= tongue is most sensitive to salt and bitter substances.
#Text=Experiment 144.
#Text=Repeat the same with some sweet or sour substances,
#Text= to show that the _edges_ of the tongue are the most sensitive to these
#Text= substances.
#Text=Experiment 145.
#Text=We often fail to distinguish between the sense of
#Text= taste and that of smell.
#Text=Chew some pure, roasted coffee, and it seems to
#Text= have a distinct taste.
#Text=Pinch the nose hard, and there is little taste.
#Text=Coffee has a powerful odor, but only a feeble taste.
#Text=The same is true of
#Text= garlic, onions, and various spices.
#Text=Experiment 146.
#Text=Light helps the sense of taste.
#Text=Shut the eyes, and
#Text= palatable foods taste insipid.
#Text=Pinch the nose, close the eyes, and see
#Text= how palatable one half of a teaspoonful of cod-liver oil becomes.
#Text=Experiment 147.
#Text=Close the nostrils, shut the eyes, and attempt to
#Text= distinguish by taste alone between a slice of an apple and one of a
#Text= potato.
#Text=
#Text= 320.
#Text=Modifications of the Sense of Taste.
#Text=Taste is modified to a
#Text= great extent by habit, education, and other circumstances.
#Text=Articles of
#Text= food that are unpleasant in early life often become agreeable in later
#Text= years.
#Text=There is occasionally a craving, especially with people of a
#Text= peculiar nervous organization, for certain unnatural articles (as chalk
#Text= and laundry starch) which are eaten without the least repugnance.
#Text=Again,
#Text= the most savory dishes may excite disgust, while the simplest articles may
#Text= have a delicious flavor to one long deprived of them.
#Text=The taste for
#Text= certain articles is certainly acquired.
#Text=This is often true of raw
#Text= tomatoes, olives, and especially of tobacco.
#Text=The organs of taste and smell may be regarded as necessary accessories of
#Text= the general apparatus of nutrition, and are, therefore, more or less
#Text= essential to the maintenance of animal life.
#Text=While taste and smell are
#Text= generally maintained until the close of life, sight and hearing are often
#Text= impaired by time, and may be altogether destroyed, the other vital
#Text=functions remaining unimpaired.
#Text=
#Text= 321.
#Text=Effect of Tobacco and Alcohol upon Taste.
#Text=It would be remarkable
#Text= if tobacco should fail to injure the sense of taste.
#Text=The effect produced
#Text= upon the tender papillæ of the tongue by the nicotine-loaded juices and
#Text= the acrid smoke tends to impair the delicate sensibility of the entire
#Text= surface.
#Text=The keen appreciation of fine flavors is destroyed.
#Text=The once
#Text= clear and enjoyable tastes of simple objects become dull and vapid; thus
#Text= highly spiced and seasoned articles of food are in demand, and then
#Text= follows continued indigestion, with all its suffering.
#Text=Again, the burning, almost caustic effect of the stronger alcoholic
#Text= drinks, and the acrid pungency of tobacco smoke, are disastrous to the
#Text= finer perceptions of both taste and odors.
#Text=
#Text=
#Text= 322.
#Text=Smell.
#Text=The sense of smell is lodged in the delicate
#Text= membrane which lines the nasal cavities.
#Text=The floor, sides, and roof of
#Text= these cavities are formed by certain bones of the cranium and the face.
#Text=Man, in common with all air-breathing animals, has two nasal cavities.
#Text=which little or no light can penetrate.
#Text=Deer, wild horses, and antelopes
#Text= probably surpass all other animals in having a vivid sense of smell.
#Text=Smell has been defined as "taste at a distance," and it is obvious that
#Text= these two senses not only form a natural group, but are clearly
#Text= associated in their physical action, especially in connection with the
#Text= perception of the flavor of food.
#Text=The sense of odor gives us information
#Text= as to the quality of food and drink, and more especially as to the quality
#Text= of the air we breathe.
#Text=Taste is at the gateway of the alimentary canal,
#Text= while smell acts as the sentinel of the respiratory tract.
#Text=Just as taste
#Text= and flavor influence nutrition by affecting the digestive process, so the
#Text= agreeable odors about us, even those of the perfumes, play an important
#Text= part in the economy of life.
#Text=
#Text=
#Text= 324.
#Text=The Sense of Sight.
#Text=The sight is well regarded as the
#Text= highest and the most perfect of all our senses.
#Text=It plays so common and so
#Text= beneficent a part in the animal economy that we scarcely appreciate this
#Text= marvelous gift.
#Text=Sight is essential not only to the simplest matters of
#Text= daily comfort and necessity, but is also of prime importance in the
#Text=culture of the mind and in the higher forms of pleasure.
#Text=It opens to us
#Text= the widest and the most varied range of observation and enjoyment.
#Text=The
#Text= pleasures and advantages it affords, directly and indirectly, have neither
#Text= cessation nor bounds.
#Text=Apart from its uses, the eye itself is an interesting and instructive
#Text= object of study.
#Text=It presents beyond comparison the most beautiful example
#Text= of design and artistic workmanship to be found in the bodily structure.
#Text=It
#Text= is the watchful sentinel and investigator of the external world.
#Text=Unlike
#Text= the senses of taste and smell we seem, by the sense of vision, to become
#Text= aware of the existence of objects which are entirely apart from us, and
#Text= which have no direct or material link connecting them with our bodies.
#Text=And
#Text= yet we are told that in vision the eye is affected by something which is
#Text= as material as any substance we taste or smell.
#Text=[NOTE.
#Text="The higher intelligence of man is intimately associated with
#Text= the perfection of the eye.
